rv.q: 'The Ferryman' is vast, a play that's formally conventional but has an ambition that's out of this world, a sense that it wants to be about EVERYTHING. And insofar as is realistically possible, it succeeds.
This is a cast without weak links.
Miss this and you’ve missed a marvel.
Running at three hours 20 minutes, this is a richly absorbing and emotionally abundant play, directed with detailed humane mastery by Sam Mendes.
Like everything else in 'The Ferryman,' those nonspeaking performers are indisputably alive.
The acting is pretty spectacular all round.
The Ferryman has lived up to the faith already invested in it.
Jez Butterworth’s vast, sprawling superbly directed (by Sam Mendes) play really does fall into that rare category – unmissable.

The lively ensemble, the subtle changes in Peter Mumford's lighting and Nick Powell's sounds that are so light and soft you barely notice them and Mendes' firm, focused grasp on the narrative's gradually growing pressure makes this new Butterworth play so engaging you won't check your watch once.
With acting like this, it's really an amazing experience, if a rather heartless one. But Butterworth's storytelling finesse carries all before it.

cn.t: Critics hail Butterworth's epic Troubles-era drama as unmissable, praising its sweeping scope and Mendes' direction. The three-hour family saga earns rave reviews and comparisons to his hit "Jerusalem."
